lawyer:
Mr. M. A. Wahab Miah, with Mr. M. Enayetur Rahim, Advocates ----- for the Petitioner. 
Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman, A. A. G. ----- for respondent No. 1
parties:
Hafeezuddin Ahmed ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Govt. of Bangladesh and another ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan, J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause why they should not be directed to implement the order passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 45 of 1991 by delivering vacant possession of the building in question, namely, House No. 5/7 Block-D, Salimullah Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka to the petitioner or such other or further order or orders passed as to this may seem fit and proper. 

 The petitioner was alloted House No. 5/7, Block-D Salimullah Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka by virtue of a registered agreement for allotment of houses executed on 9th February, 1960 and subsequently possession was delivered to him and since that time the petitioner had been in possession of the House in question with his family members-After the liberation of Bangladesh the petitioner was ousted from the House in question by some armed miscreants and since then the same is being occupied by unauthorised persons. The petitioner never left the country nor gave any option for Pakistan. He was an employee of Bangladesh Railway and though he was out of service for some time he resumed his duties on 20.9.1982 and thereafter he retired from service on 1.10.1990. Now he has been drawing his pension as a retired employee of Bangladesh Railway. In spite of giving representations, both orally and in writing to the respondents the concerned Ministry failed to give possession of the house to the petitioner by way of evicting the unauthorised occupant and ultimately the property was Included in the list of abandoned buildings published by the Ministry of Works as per provisions of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. The petitioner filed an application before the Court of Settlement under section 7 of the said Ordinance for excluding the house in question from the list of Abandoned Buildings and the said application was registered as Case No. 45/91 (Ka) 180-Block-D, Mohammadpur, Dhaka. 

 3. The Government contested the said case without filing any written statement denying the material statements made in the application filed in the Court of Settlement. The petitioner having appeared personally before the Court of Settlement, the service book and the service record of. the petitioner having been called for from the Finance Adviser and Chief Accountant (East) of the Bangladesh Railway, Chittagong was duly produced before the Court of Settlement. The Court of Settlement after hearing the learned Advocate of the petitioner as well as the Government lawyer and on perusal of the service Book and other connected records produced by the Railway Authority being satisfied as to the bonafide and genuineness of the petitioner's claim by its judgment and order dated 30th day of September, 1992 allowed the application and excluded the property from the list of abandoned buildings and directed that the petitioner be restored to possession of the house. It was also found by the Court of Settlement that the petitioner was an employee of the Bangladesh Railway and be retired from service in 1990 and now he is a pension holder and the property is not an abandoned property but it was wrongly listed in the 'ka' list. 

 4. After the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement the petitioner approached the respondents and thereafter filed written application on 5.12.92 to the Minister in-Charge of the Ministry of Works, Secretary, Ministry of Works, Chairman, Abandoned Properties and Management Board requesting them to implement the decision of the Court of Settlement by handing over vacant possession of the house in question to him but no step has yet been taken for giving delivery of possession of the house to the petitioner. The petitioner against filed applications to the Secretary of the Ministry of Works on 20.12.92 and 31.12.92 making similar prayer but to no result. Ultimately the petitioner received a letter issued under the signature of the Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Works that the Ministry has written to the Divisional Commissioner and Chairman of the Abandoned Properties Management Board, Shegun Bagicha for sending the record to the Ministry in respect of the house in question for placing the same before the Writ Committee of the Ministry. Having failed to get delivery of possession of the house in question even after the judgment and order passed in his favour by the Court of Settlement, the petitioner being aggrieved moved this court and, obtained the present rule. 

 5. Mr. M. A Wahab Miah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that the Court of Settlement after due consideration of the evidence and materials on record decided that the property in question was wrongly treated as abandoned and hence directed for the exclusion of the same from the list of the abandoned buildings with a further direction for the restoration of possession of the building to the petitioner but the possession of the property has not yet been restored to the petitioner and in that view of the matter a direction from this court is necessary to be given for restoration of possession of property in question to the petitioner in terms of the judgment and order of the court of Settlement. It is submitted that the Court of Settlement has been constituted by the Government under the provision of section 7 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 and the Government is under legal obligation to, implement, execute the decision given by the said court of settlement and as such for the inaction on the part of the officials of the Government in not implementing/executing the decision passed by the Court of Settlement a mandate from this Hon'ble court seems to be imperative for the implementation and execution of the order of the Court of Settlement. 

 7. Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondent no. 1 submitted that the respondents have not expressed their unwillingness to hand over possession of the houses in question to the rightful claimant but the matter is being delayed as a lot of formalities ate to be observed before handing over of the house consequent on the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement. Without appreciating that some time is necessary for the verification of the record and identification of the claimant the petitioner has rushed to this court and hence the learned Assistant Attorney General submitted that the application being pre-mature the petitioner is not entitled to any relief in the same. The learned Assistant Attorney General further submitted that before seeking relief by way of filing the writ application no demand for justice notice was issued and served on the respondents enabling them to take necessary step in the matter. Whatever might be the point raised, the learned Assistant Attorney General found it difficult to justify the in action on the part of the Government in carrying out of the order of the Court of Settlement. 

 8. From the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement passed on 30th September, 1982 and after hearing both the parties it appears that the learned Court of Settlement after due consideration of the fact and circumstances of the case was clearly of the opinion that the case house is not an abandoned building and it was wrongly included in the list of abandoned building and hence should be excluded from the 'Ka' list. Direction was also been given by the Court of Settlement for the restoration of the possession of the building to the petitioner. The order of the Court of Settlement for restoration of the property in question to the petitioner is final and binding on the respondents in view of section 10 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance 1985, (54 of 1985). Though no specific provision has been made in the Ordinance for the execution of the order of the Court of Settlement, we are of the view that the Government is under legal obligation to give effect to the decision of the Court of Settlement. From the averments made in the affidavit in opposition and the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney General it appears that the decision of the court of settlement has not been challenged before any higher forum and that the respondents are not unwilling to give effect of the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement. Since the judgment and order has been passed by the learned Court of Settlement after hearing both the parties it is not desirable that the matter of handing over of the possession of the house in question to the petitioner will be kept in abeyance for an unlimited period. We also do not find sub stance in the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney General that the writ petition is not maintainable for not issuing demand for justice of notice to the respondents as the authority turned deaf cars to the representations made by the petitioner for obtaining delivery of possession after the judgment and order of the court of settlement. 

 9. In view of the above, we are of the view that the respondents are required by law to implement the decision of the Court of Settlement and restore the property in question to the petitioner giving effect to the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement.
